title: The War Moves East
subtitle: The Ukrainian counterstrokes, a fighting withdrawal and the violence in Lwów
author: R.G. Cruise
summary: Soviet counterattacks in western Ukraine failed to destroy the German penetration but helped preserve a fighting withdrawal. In Lwów, NKVD prison murders were followed by German occupation, antisemitic incitement and the July 1 pogrom.
body:
Rain on the roads east

The Southwestern Front’s morning report for July 1 ended with a detail easily lost in accounts of the great tank battles: rain was falling and the unpaved roads were washed out. Above that observation stood the condition of an army group in retreat. The 5th Army was preparing another attack before withdrawing toward the Sluch. The Sixth, Twenty-sixth and 12th Armies were moving through successive positions farther south. Front headquarters had no current information locating the Fourth and 8th Mechanized Corps. The Fifteenth had been reported around Bilyi Kamin. A war often remembered through spectacular tank numbers was being decided by the ability to move exhausted formations along roads that were becoming harder to use. [1] The retreat followed a series of armored battles around Lutsk, Dubno and Brody. Soviet counterattacks had not destroyed the German penetration or restored the frontier. They had, however, made Army Group South’s progress different from the devastating encirclement achieved around Minsk. German forces were advancing through western Ukraine, but significant Soviet armies remained capable of withdrawing, defending and attacking again. The distinction mattered to both sides. It bought the Soviet command opportunities while leaving it with severely damaged mechanized formations and the continuing danger of a breakthrough toward the old fortified line. [2] [3] Behind the retreating armies, Lwów had fallen to the Germans on June 30. Soviet security forces had murdered prisoners before leaving. The new occupiers and local collaborators used the discovery of their bodies to incite violence against Jews. On July 1 the city was experiencing a pogrom, making the change of military control immediately lethal for civilians. [4] Withdrawal offered no common refuge to soldiers and civilians. Kirponos could still order armies toward another defensive line, but people left in Lwów confronted institutions that selected victims by political status or Jewish identity. The military and civilian crises intersected at the transfer of power without sharing the same causes. The Soviet counterattacks help explain why troops could leave the city; the decisions of Soviet security personnel, German occupiers and local participants explain why prisoners and Jewish inhabitants were killed. Neither history can be made intelligible by treating the other as background noise.

Why the southern advance was different

Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt’s Army Group South had one principal armored striking force, Ewald von Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group. Walter von Reichenau’s 6th Army advanced on the northern part of the Ukrainian sector, while Carl-Heinrich von Stülpnagel’s 17th Army fought farther south toward and beyond Lwów. The German plan sought to destroy Soviet forces west of the Dnieper, using the mobile penetration to cut their retreat. But unlike Army Group Center, Rundstedt did not begin with two panzer groups placed to make a comparable double envelopment around the main opposing deployment. The different arrangement was a constraint on method, not merely a difference in the length of the arrows. [3] Mikhail Kirponos commanded the Soviet Southwestern Front, with Mikhail Potapov’s 5th Army on its northern wing and Ivan Muzychenko’s Sixth around the Lwów sector. Fyodor Kostenko’s Twenty-sixth and Pavel Ponedelin’s Twelfth extended the front toward the Carpathians and the Romanian approaches. These armies were threatened differently as the German penetration developed. Potapov had to contain the thrust through Volhynia and protect the routes toward Rovno, now Rivne. The armies farther south had to avoid remaining too long in the westward projection around Lwów while German mobile forces moved beyond their northern flank. [5] [6] The operational geography was more intricate than an open Ukrainian plain. The Western Bug marked the initial crossing; the Styr, Ikva and Horyn divided subsequent routes. Around Brody and Berestechko, smaller rivers ran through marshy valleys with limited bridges and causeways. The 15th Mechanized Corps’ after-action report listed five significant water obstacles in its intended attack zone and described swampy approaches, restricted roads and commanding ground held by the enemy. Tanks were numerous, but places where they could cross and deploy were not. [7] Kleist’s mobile forces could gain ground without clearing the Soviet formations on either side of their advance. The roads behind the leading tanks still had to carry ammunition, fuel and repair support. Attacks from the north and south threatened that traffic and forced the Germans to turn units against the attackers. Blau’s account records repeated Soviet counterattacks and progress below German expectations. This gives the disruption a documented operational meaning without claiming that Kirponos had achieved his larger purpose: the German penetration survived, while the Soviet mechanized corps suffered losses they would carry into the next defense. [3]

The corps that had tanks but lacked a complete force

The counterattack program described in the study for June 25 required attacks from opposite sides of the German penetration. The Eighth and 15th Mechanized Corps were central to the southern blow; the Ninth and Nineteenth were assigned to Potapov’s northern grouping. The 4th Corps also supplied forces and fought in the Lwów sector. These were substantial formations on organizational charts, but their inventories cannot be added together and treated as the strength of one simultaneous battle. Units arrived at different times, received changing tasks and sometimes operated apart from their parent corps. [8] The 15th Corps offers a particularly revealing case because its commander’s subsequent report explains what was missing. The corps entered the war under Ignaty Karpezo. Its 37th Tank Division had an incomplete motorized infantry regiment far from the division and without transport. Some artillery lacked the tractors necessary to move it. The 212th Motorized Division had men but almost no vehicles for carrying them, their weapons or their supplies. Corps signals and engineer units were still being formed and trained. A formation could therefore contain modern tanks while lacking the infantry, bridging and communications needed to make those tanks effective. [7] The corps report places a precise delay within that larger organizational problem. The order requiring an attack at seven on June 25 reportedly reached 15th Corps at 8:30, after the prescribed start. This sequence identifies a transmission failure that an explanation based simply on slow execution would miss. The same account describes marsh-bound movement, artillery arriving from training areas and changes of assembly position. It is retrospective testimony from a command explaining its actions, so its claims require that attribution; nonetheless, the comparison with the front’s dated order establishes a concrete discrepancy between the schedule imposed and the time at which the corps said it received it. [7] [9] Command itself was disrupted by attack. The corps report dates the bombing that incapacitated Karpezo to the evening of June 26 and states that his deputy, Colonel Yermolayev, took over. That dated record is preferable to carrying Karpezo’s name across the entire battle or assuming that a change of commander occurred on the invasion’s first day. German air action mattered here not only because it might destroy tanks. It could wound the people organizing a corps, displace its headquarters and consume time needed to coordinate an attack. [7]

The counterstroke reaches the German communications

On June 27, one part of the counterstroke was already advancing while another was still reorganizing. The Southwestern Front’s midnight report stated that the 8th Mechanized Corps had begun its attack from the Radziwiłłów area at nine that morning, with Dubno as its end-of-day objective. Its leading detachment reportedly passed Sytne at 11:30 without meeting the enemy. Meanwhile, the 15th Corps was around Toporiv, preparing its own attack toward Berestechko. Headquarters could report progress, but the entries do not describe the simultaneous converging blow demanded by the plan. [10] A group from Ryabyshev’s 8th Corps, associated with commissar Nikolai Popel and elements of the Twelfth and 34th Tank Divisions, penetrated toward Dubno and threatened German communications. Aleksey Isaev’s reconstruction identifies the disruption while distinguishing it from Popel’s more expansive retrospective claims about entry into the city and captured senior officers. German forces, including Hube’s 16th Panzer Division, redirected against the penetration and isolated the Soviet group. The sequence connects achievement and vulnerability: reaching a valuable route imposed a problem on the enemy, while sustaining that position required connections and support the Soviet attackers could not preserve. [11] The 15th Corps’ parallel effort shows why the wider counteroffensive did not develop around that penetration. Its report describes an intended advance of forty kilometers toward Berestechko, across a zone with several difficult water obstacles. The staff considered the available strength inadequate for the assigned task and judged that a narrower attack against German communications was more realistic. Orders to withdraw and then resume the offensive further disrupted the corps’ preparations. These retrospective explanations are partly a commander’s account of failure and must be read as such. They are nonetheless unusually specific about the relation between the task, time and available means. [7] On June 28, the 10th Tank Division could not force the Ostrivka crossing over a causeway under German artillery and antitank fire. Yermolayev sent a liaison officer to obtain support from the attached 8th Tank Division. The officer’s car was hit and burned; the wounded messenger reached the division through fields and gullies. Two tanks sent on the same mission were also set on fire. The account makes the command problem tangible. Cooperation depended on a messenger physically crossing ground the enemy could already fire across. [7] The 37th Tank Division’s difficulty near Stanyslavchyk illustrates the interaction of terrain, fire and coordination. Vehicles attempting to bypass a bridge entered marshy ground and became vulnerable to artillery; the corps subsequently withdrew from the exposed area between rivers. The report’s explanation cannot be reduced to the relative quality of opposing tanks. Crossings channeled movement, supporting arms and messages had to traverse threatened ground, and local setbacks affected the feasibility of the wider assignment. Those relationships explain how a formation with substantial equipment could lose its capacity to deliver an effective blow before every vehicle had been destroyed. [7]

A timetable for retreat, not a recovered front

At eleven on the night of June 30, Kirponos issued a new program. The Southwestern Front was to withdraw toward the Korosten, Novograd-Volynskiy, Shepetovka, Starokonstantinov and Proskurov fortified regions by July 9, while holding an intermediate line until July 6. The order acknowledged German control of the Dubno–Ostrog–Rovno area after stubborn fighting. It also recognized danger from the north, where German forces had reached Bobruisk, and from concentrations in northeastern Romania. The southern armies were no longer dealing only with the battle immediately in front of them. Their flanks belonged to a widening campaign. [5] The withdrawal was assigned stages rather than a single destination. Potapov’s 5th Army was to begin moving after darkness on July 1, reach intermediate positions on the Styr and Horyn, and arrive at the Sluch by the morning of the 5th. The 6th Army received its own sequence through Ostrog, Kremenets and Volochisk. The Twenty-sixth and 12th Armies had routes farther south. Mechanized corps were to regroup behind them, and aviation was ordered to protect their movement while continuing to strike the German penetration. These dates establish what the command wanted to achieve. They do not demonstrate that all the intermediate positions were reached or held as prescribed. [5] The morning summary on July 1 shows the first reality against which that program had to operate. The 5th Army was still combining an attack south toward Mizoch with preparations to withdraw. A German attempt to cross the Horyn the previous afternoon was reported repulsed. The 6th Army was moving through positions east of Lwów, while the Twenty-sixth withdrew from the approaches south of the city. The front could still describe an army-level operation, but it admitted that the whereabouts of two mechanized corps were unknown. This was more coherent than the Western Front’s condition around Minsk, yet far from an orderly march by intact formations. [1] Kirponos’s receiving line also required a different use of his surviving weapons. The order gave artillery and antitank assets priority in organizing the field defense around the fortified regions. Concrete works could strengthen troops who reached them, but they could not replace a force capable of covering the approaches and neighboring sectors. For the artillerymen, withdrawal meant getting guns and ammunition over the intervening roads; for headquarters, it meant arranging those arrivals before the enemy penetrated the line. The works and the retreating army had to be joined in time. [5] The same order assigned the 49th Rifle Corps a task distinct from the retreat of the forward armies. Its 190th and 197th Rifle Divisions were to march from Volochisk on the morning of July 1 and occupy fortifications around Liakhovtsy, Bazaliya and Sharlaevka that evening. Kirponos was trying to put troops into the receiving position while the battered mobile formations moved behind it. The corps offered the possibility of a defended destination rather than merely another line toward which exhausted units could be told to withdraw. Whether that possibility became effective depended on arrivals and coordination: the order also allotted separate routes and successive assembly areas to the Fourth, Eighth and 15th Mechanized Corps. Preserving those formations required space on the roads as well as permission to retreat. [5] For German headquarters, the southern fighting was already a warning against assuming uniform results across the front. Blau’s official study describes repeated Soviet counterattacks and an advance below German expectations. That is a contemporary expectation reconstructed from the German records, not a license to invent a deadline for Kiev. By July 1, the Germans had gained substantial ground and defeated the immediate Soviet counteroffensive; they had not destroyed the Southwestern Front in a counterpart to the Minsk encirclement. Both parts of that judgment are necessary. [3]

Lwów’s prisons and the change of occupier

The German capture of Lwów, today Lviv, exposed the bodies of prisoners killed by Soviet security personnel during the retreat. The city’s Łąckiego prison was one site of the murders. Research presented by Lviv’s Center for Urban History dates the beginning of the killings there to the night of June 23–24 and relates them to the Soviet decision to eliminate political detainees rather than permit their release as the Germans approached. The victims of Soviet repression came from several communities. Their murder was a crime committed by the Soviet authorities, and the hurried military withdrawal does not alter that responsibility. [12] The discovery also created an opportunity for German propaganda. Bodies were displayed, relatives searched for missing people, and Jews were forced into the work of removing and arranging the dead. The occupiers and nationalist activists falsely assigned collective responsibility for Soviet crimes to the city’s Jews, although Jews had themselves been among the victims of Soviet repression. By forcing Jews to expose the bodies before gathering crowds, the organizers joined physical coercion to a public accusation. The corpses were evidence of NKVD murder; the people compelled to handle them were being persecuted for their identity. The political use of the prisoners’ deaths depended on obscuring that distinction. [12] The political transition in the city was also contested within the invading coalition. On June 30, Yaroslav Stetsko proclaimed a Ukrainian state in the name of Stepan Bandera’s wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists, the OUN-B. The declaration sought to use the German advance to establish national authority. German leaders had their own plans for exploiting and governing Ukraine, and would reject the proclamation and arrest its leaders. Those later measures do not mean that OUN-B activists had been uninvolved in cooperation with the Germans or anti-Jewish persecution at the moment of conquest. [13] The OUN-B’s ambitions for statehood did not prevent its activists from advancing an antisemitic political program. Breitman and Goda’s archival study connects Stetsko’s statements and the nationalist proclamation to cooperation with Germany. Those records establish aims and political alignment; Himka’s examination of the militia and the pogrom supplies evidence of participation in violence. Keeping the two kinds of evidence together shows how a movement seeking recognition from the occupier could help persecute a community while possessing no German guarantee that its own state would survive. [13] [14]

The pogrom on July 1

John-Paul Himka’s study of the Lviv pogrom distinguishes the roles of German forces, the Ukrainian nationalist militia and the participating urban crowd. German occupation created the setting and encouraged violence; militia members seized Jews and brought them into the sites of abuse; civilians joined in robbery, humiliation and assault. The crowd included both Poles and Ukrainians. Naming these participants is more accurate than assigning guilt to an entire national population, and it prevents the category “local violence” from obscuring the role of the occupiers. [14] The violence targeted women as well as men and included sexual assault and public degradation. Jews forced to handle the prison dead were attacked under an accusation they could not answer by proving their innocence, because the accusation concerned their identity rather than any individual act. German forces also carried out shootings. Himka’s analysis therefore resists a clean division between a civilian mob and an entirely separate official killing operation: their actions interacted, although particular acts still require specific attribution. [14] The pogrom’s death toll is less certain than its occurrence and perpetrators. The Holocaust Memorial Museum gives at least several hundred victims, possibly more, and warns that familiar totals combine the pogrom with German executions over a longer part of July. Four thousand should therefore not be presented as an agreed count for July 1 alone. Separating those events preserves their chronology without diminishing the crime. [4]

Counting different events

Why familiar totals can mislead

Some estimates combine the early pogrom, prison shootings and later executions. A total for that wider sequence cannot be assigned automatically to the mob violence of July 1. The event is securely documented even where its exact death toll remains uncertain. [4]

The surviving photographs make some acts visible but cannot supply a complete record of the city. German cameramen filmed and photographed the violence for propaganda, preserving evidence that requires attention to who selected and framed it. Testimonies identify experiences outside those frames, while the militia and military records help establish institutional roles. Himka compares these materials rather than treating a single image as a census of perpetrators or victims. That approach also prevents the crowd’s participation from becoming an excuse for the occupying authorities, whose orders and protection helped make the attacks possible. [14] [4]

Riga and the unequal movement of the war

Far to the north, German troops occupied Riga on July 1 as Army Group North expanded its position on the Western Dvina. The evening German map shows an advance distributed across several crossings and routes, not one uniform line sweeping through Latvia. The Soviet Northwestern Front’s intelligence report that evening described German concentrations near the river, reconnaissance between Pļaviņas and Krāslava, and movement from the Jēkabpils–Līvāni sector toward Madona and Gulbene. It also recorded air reconnaissance around Tallinn and Pskov. The pressure was spreading beyond the initial river crossings toward the next defensive area. [15] [16] Riga’s loss widened the routes available to Army Group North while the Soviet Baltic armies sought another defensive position. In the center, German infantry continued reducing the Minsk pockets. The southwestern armies faced a third situation: Kirponos had ordered a staged retreat, with counterattacks still covering parts of the movement. These differences affected the next German decisions. A force already trapped required reduction; an army withdrawing in order could preserve enough strength to fight at the next river or fortified region. On July 1 the Southwestern Front remained dangerous because it had not ceased to function. [2] The cost of keeping that front alive was already visible in its mobile formations. The 15th Corps’ report described missing transport and engineer support before battle, disrupted command during it, and withdrawals from exposed crossings afterward. The morning summary then placed the corps behind the armies while admitting that headquarters could not locate two others. Kirponos retained armies capable of movement, but not an undamaged armored reserve ready to repeat the first week’s efforts. The retreat preserved an operational problem for the Germans while passing severe weaknesses to the next Soviet defense. [5] [7] [3] By July 1, the German penetration in Ukraine had survived the counterattacks, and Soviet troops were leaving the western borderlands. Their withdrawal remained organized enough to offer hope of another line, but communications, transport and armored strength had been badly damaged. In Lwów, Soviet prison murder had been followed by German occupation and anti-Jewish violence. The change of rulers offered the city’s Jewish inhabitants no safety. Two days later, Stalin would publicly call for national resistance. The next study examines the resources, institutions and coercion behind that appeal.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations identify the evidence for each passage. Soviet orders and reports are read in published Russian transcriptions; their assignments, enemy-loss claims and admissions of missing information are distinguished from confirmed outcomes. German situation sheets record headquarters’ information, and the postwar official histories are retrospective interpretations. Holocaust research combines institutional studies, perpetrator records and survivor testimony. Individual experiences are attributed, and later consequences are dated separately. The documentary material is consulted through published editions and transcriptions, not the underlying archival files.
